subsubtopic: CALL FOR RETURN OF CAPITAL PUNISHMENT FOR CERTAIN MURDERS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. One of the accused killers of Emanuel Jaques, the Toronto shoeshine boy who was so brutally murdered last year, admitted to a court last Friday that if capital punishment had been in effect at the time, the boy may not have been killed. As the law now stands, these deranged individuals will more than likely once again endanger our society with their presence in just a matter of years. Therefore, for the sake of preventing such killing, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle):
That this House reinstate forthwith capital punishment in respect of sex-related killings as well as all other first degree, premeditated murders.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion dealing with an important matter of pressing necessity.
In reply to a question put by the Leader of the Opposition yesterday, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) stated the following:
One problem with cutting the federal sales tax is that we cannot be sure that the reduction would be passed on to the consumer.

That the House immediately enjoin the government to issue a rebate to consumers-a compensatory discount-on consumer goods and thus stimulate the economy.

subsubtopic: RESTORATION OF GRAIN SHIPPING SERVICE TO MANITOBA ELEVATORS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to propose a motion of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that on CNR's Inwood subdivision, in the Interlake area of Manitoba, there has been no train service since last December, with the consequence that farmers of the area are now being forced to haul their grain by truck, up to 60 miles in some cases, to elevators on other branch lines on which there is service, and in view of the fact that all storage areas are full and some grain is
March 7, 1978

even stored out in the open, where it will rot if it is not soon shipped, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie):
That this House direct the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board to act immediately to restore grain quotas and grain shipping service to the elevators at Fisher Branch, Manitoba, on CNR's Inwood subdivision, and in view of the fact that this line is slated for probable abandonment in 1979, that the government immediately establish the Prairie Rail Authority so that the off-line loading experiment can be instituted at Fisher Branch, as recommended by the Hall commission, and the farmers of the area can continue to deliver their grain to the elevators at Fisher Branch with the assurance that it will be shipped out of the Interlake via commercial truck to CPR's Arborg rail line, financially assisted and co-ordinated by the federal government through the Prairie Rail Authority.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Finance. Reports emanating from money markets around the world indicate that while the Canadian government has been attempting to defend the dollar, it has been buffeted by certain international investors. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the information related by the hon. member has no basis in fact. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Yesterday, the minister announced that a U.S. citizen, R. Sherrell, was granted permission to enter Canada to become president of the Insurance Corporation of British Columbia, with an annual salary of $80,000 a year. -the fact remains that an adequate search in Canada was not made and there is evidence that at least one qualified Canadian was available.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subtopic: ACCEPTANCE BY CANADA OF U.S. CITIZENS FOR CANADIAN JOBS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first and foremost, 1 think I should point out that the Price Waterhouse Company, who usually do an excellent job in this area, flubbed in this particular case and did not contact our Manpower and Immigration offices. It was not until the day before we heard that an announcement was to be made that we contacted cabinet minister for the province of British Columbia and indicated the difficulties involved, that we had not been contacted, did not know whether an adequate search had been made, and wanted to be satisfied that that had taken place.
On the basis of evidence that we had, we were satisfied that an adequate search had not been made, so we refused to grant the necessary points to Mr. Sherrell-who, incidentally, is the innocent party in this situation. Following that, I met with the selection committee of ICBC and went through, with them and representatives from Price Waterhouse, the number of candidates they had contacted across Canada, some 274 or 275. I was satisfied that they had not made an adequate search. They had not done any advertising east of British Columbia other than one ad in the Globe and Mail.
Having been given all this information and the present dilemma that the company finds itself in, namely, with $400 million in premiums and the necessity of finding a person for this particular job, I think the fact that they appointed a Canadian as chairman of the board is a direct result of the intervention we made. I was satisfied it was an appropriate time to exercise discretion and allow Mr. Sherrell to take this particular job and, at the same time, put provincial authorities on notice that in future they will have to go through the procedures or they will be more embarrassed than they have been in this case.

Some consideration is being given to having that question examined by the Rights and Immunities Committee, which is not reconstituted. As a preliminary step, that committee will have to be reconstituted and then consulted to determine two things. First, it will have to determine whether it is disposed to examine the matter within roughly the terms of reference proposed by the hon. member for Yukon, and, second, the format of those discussions or examination, because the work of that committee in the past has very much been a study of problems with an effort to come to some consensus in the form of a recommendation to the House on a particular matter. That was done in the matter of questions concerning subjects that are before the courts.
If that is to be the basis of the study of this committee, which is yet to be determined, it will be possible for me to continue to preside over it. On the other hand, if it is desired that witnesses be called before the committee and that a more formal type of hearing be entered into, it will be difficult for me to continue to preside.
Therefore, two questions have to be resolved. The first is whether the Rights and Immunities Committee, having been reconstituted, is prepared to study it and try to report back in a short space of time and, second, the format of examination of it. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT POLICY

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext: Pursuant to Standing Order 32(1 )(k) and Standing Order 58(11), proceedings on this motion will expire at the ordinary hour of adjournment this evening.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to engage the House of Commons in a debate which will deal with one of the most important matters that can affect our future as a modern, industrialized country. It is clear to all of us including, even though he will not admit it, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), that this country today is in a state of very real economic crisis.
We have more than one million unemployed. We have a number of Canadian plants and industries across the country that would find jobs for those Canadians but they are operating so much under capacity because of low demand and low stimulus in the economy that those jobs are not in existence.
We have a situation where the Government of Canada continues to pretend it is engaging in restraint but in fact it is engaging in the worst kind of governmental extravagance. We also have a situation where the government's growth projections are clearly wrong on the future of the Canadian economy.
What troubles most of us is that the Government of Canada, dealing with short-term immediate problems and dealing with this crisis of unemployment, seems not to care at all about the plight of the Canadian unemployed.
The Minister of Finance continues to refuse to bring in a budget. He does that even though the treasurer of the province of Ontario, who is today bringing in his own budget, has been urging the minister in the strongest possible terms to give some meaning and content to the agreement of the first ministers' conference earlier this year and to bring in a budget that will give credence to those measures that were agreed on by the premiers when they met here in Ottawa.
As 1 have said here before, the real reason the government does not want to bring in a budget is a political reason. It is
March 7, 1978

doing everything it can to keep discussion of the economy of Canada off the floor of the House of Commons of Canada. Ministers continue to refuse to bring in any real stimulus to the economy and they continue to refuse to exercise any real restraint over the activities of the Government of Canada. Instead, they try to hide the seriousness of the problem.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) goes around the country pretending unemployment doesn't matter. Well, let him try it! It certainly matters, especially to those one million Canadians who cannot find work. We find also, in that department, an example of the shameful behaviour of the government inasmuch as the basis of reporting has been juggled so as to conceal the effects of lay-offs. Until last month the department used to issue a report showing lay-offs in industries where lay-offs involved more than 20 people in a month. Now, so embarrassing does the government find these statistics that the basis has been changed in an effort to hide the real face of unemployment, to conceal its real impact upon the province of Ontario and upon other provinces.
Moreover, the government continues to refuse to state clearly the economic policy it is pursuing in relation to the Canadian dollar. Last week the government announced it was going down to the SEC. This week, judging by the interest rates, we will probably have to go to HFC!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext: Sir, the economic crisis in Canada is the result of the worst decade of economic management in the history of this country, a situation which is entirely consistent with a government which is the worst federal government since Confederation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext:
In part, also, it is due to the complete failure of the government to give any priority to economic policy and the consequent failure to establish any coherent national economic strategy to prepare us for a much tougher, much more competitive future. The absence of any economic strategy has become clear most dramatically and most dangerously in our preparation for the GATT negotiations at Geneva.
It is difficult enough for Canada going into GATT negotiations because we are, relatively, one of the smaller economies in the world. But our problems have been aggravated in the extreme by entering into these negotiations, negotiations which will require commitments which could affect us for years, without knowing ourselves what we want to do, where we want to specialize, that direction we want our growth as a nation to take in the decades ahead.
No one pretends it is easy to establish a comprehensive national economic strategy. But ease of accomplishment is not the issue. The government has failed even to try to make a start and nobody can forgive it for failing to begin the hard work of developing such a strategy. We are paying for that failure now, and the government has an immediate obligation
Research and Development
to begin the hard work of developing a genuine national economic strategy for Canada.
Naturally, an essential element of that strategy will be the frankest, fullest possible consultation with the other partners in the Canadian community-the provinces, organized labour, business and so on. But one element in any national economic strategy is already clear: we must emphasize high technology, research and development industries if we are to compete and grow in the modern world.
We are fortunate among nations in the extent and wealth of our natural resource base. But we have to face the fact that other countries, too, enjoy wealthy natural resource bases, including countries whose wage rates and productivity levels are much more competitive than ours. So we have also to use the other great resource of Canada-human ingenuity and innovation. We have to use our brains as well as our brawn as a nation or we shall not be able to compete in the modern world.
[ Translation]
The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development published recently a list of the 110 most important technical discoveries since World War II. None of them was made in Canada. This exemplifies one of the most disquieting problems facing Canada today. At a time when progress depends largely on technology, Canada discourages research and development. Yet, technical discoveries would play an essential part in achieving all our economic objectives. They are the key to a new growth and new job opportunities. They are the key to industrial effectiveness and, by way of consequence, to greater price stability. They are the key to a better trade balance and a stronger value for the Canadian dollar.
Our problem is twofold. First, our technical discoveries are decreasing in number. Second, we are lagging more and more behind our competitors. Which means that in the area of technical discoveries, the gap between Canada and the other developed nations is forever widening. Had Canada last year applied an adequate research and development policy, nearly 50,000 scientists, engineers, research planners and other technicians would be working in the Canadian sector of manufactured industries, thus ensuring greater prospects for our economic future.

So that gap, instead of narrowing, is growing wider. The OECD has recently compared the gross expenditures of various nations on research and development as a percentage of the gross national product of those nations. In the period from 1965 to 1975 to which the study applies, the OECD selected average for all member countries remained the same at 1.6 per cent. For Canada, in that period, the percentage dropped from 1.1 per cent to 0.9 per cent.
Three points must be made about that situation. First, by investing less than one per cent of our gross national product in innovation Canada has the worst record of any western nation, the worst in the western world. Second, the Committee on

March 7, 1978
Research and Development
Science Policy of the other place set a goal of 2.5 per cent of the GNP as being a proper national objective. Not only are we falling behind other nations, we are falling behind the goal which our own advisers have established. Third, while the OECD average has remained the same, Canada's investment in innovation has been dropping. The countries whose investment has increased include West Germany, Japan and even Italy. And all our major competitors invest considerably more in innovation than does Canada. That fact comes home in our trade.
Today we are running a $10 billion deficit in high technology manufactured goods. What is most dangerous about this deficit is that it is not remaining static-it is deepening. In the years before 1970 we ran a deficit of about $1 billion in trade in those goods. Since then there has been a straight-line trend downward. This means that Canada's situation is going to get seriously worse. We shall fall even farther behind in innovation unless there is a change in the approach and policy of the government.
Investment in innovation is not just something it would be nice to do. It is not part of an international game of keeping up with the Joneses. Unless we innovate, our trade problems will grow more severe, unemployment will get worse, prices will continue to rise.
General Electric in the United States recently commissioned an analysis of output, employment, and price behaviour over the last 25 years in high technology and low technology industries in the United States. Three facts stand out from that analysis. First, high technology products provide a positive trade balance while low technology products do not. Second, high technology industries grew in that period almost three times as fast as low technology industries, and their productivity was twice as high. Finally, in high technology industries manufacturing prices rose much more slowly, while employment grew almost nine times as fast as it did in low technology industries. So, in terms of jobs, lower prices, better trade, and faster growth we need to invest in innovation as a nation.
I think two comparisons with the situation in the United States dramatize the changes in attitude and in policy which are necessary for Canada. The first of those relates to research which is done outside government by the industries of the two nations. In the United States-and this is a startling, sobering fact-three companies, General Motors, IBM, and Ford, each on their own spend more on research and development than all Canadian companies taken together spend on innovation in Canada. In other words, each of three major companies there invest more, in total budget, in innovation than the total of Canadian companies invest in innovation in this country. That indicates a failure on the part of Canadian industry which we in this House of Commons have to recognize is related in part to the fact that much of our industry has head offices elsewhere, which tends to attract research elsewhere.
The second comparison is that the Government of Canada in its last budget took what amounts for this government to a great leap forward. In fact it was more like a stumble in the dark. The government brought the tax credit for research and development up to 10 per cent for those areas where unemployment is the most serious. In other words, a 10 per cent tax credit for innovation is the highest the Canadian government will go, and that only in the most strictly limited circumstances. A 10 per cent tax credit is where the United States starts. They start at our highest level, and that is one of the reasons for the difference in the interest in innovation by industry in the two countries. That indicates again an absolute failure on the part of this government to commit itself to innovation in this country.
These are not new words. These are not new warnings. The Canadian research community, and virtually every study into the question of innovation and research, have been warning about the dangers of the failure of Canada to encourage research and development. Now the research community-and 1 think this is important-and others who are concerned in the country, are joined explicitly by the ten premiers of Canada.
1 think the whole country was very much amused by the degree of enthusiasm and eagerness with which this government, which has added so much to confrontation and disunity in this country during its ten years in office, claimed credit for bringing together the ten premiers. I applaud the government for finally doing that. I think it is important that Canadians note that last year, when the need to meet was most urgent, was the first year in several that the Government of Canada failed to convene a meeting of first ministers. However, I congratulate the government for finally catching up and taking the initiative it should have taken. Calling a meeting is not difficult, but acting on the results of that meeting is the true test of commitment and concern on the part of a federal government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext: And making proposals.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Indeed, as my colleague, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), points out very appropriately, making proposals is also a very important test. The most remarkable aspect of the first ministers' conference was that all the serious proposals came from the provinces.
I should make one exception. There was one specific proposal which came from the federal government. That contained a long list of projects proposed by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) which included, prominently, the Kitimat pipeline, which his colleagues two weeks later turned around and scuttled. One specific agreement, which came about largely because of the inspiration of the government of Ontario but which also had the support of other premiers, found its way into the statement of conclusions, and I would like to read it into the record. The following is an agreement between the Government of Canada and the provincial governments:

March 7, 1978

Joint steps will be taken to improve tax incentives or credits to industry for research and development, the expansion of employment opportunities in these areas, and increase dissemination and application of existing technology.
That was the commitment. The question now is, where is the action by the Government of Canada? The question for the federal government now is, will the federal government honour the commitment it gave to the provinces and to the research community of Canada?
Will the minister himself, who is in the House today, urge his colleagues, and particularly the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), to bring in a budget as soon as possible to provide those tax incentives or those tax credits? If the government is afraid of a budget, as I presume it is, will it take some other action immediately to carry out the will and the agreement of the first ministers, and to begin to make Canada competitive again in a high technology world?
I understand that the minister will be speaking later today. I hope to be able to hear him. I certainly look forward to his spelling out the initiatives-and the time-frame for enacting those initiatives-which the Government of Canada intends to take both to honour the agreement at the first ministers' meeting as well as to begin progress toward making this country competitive again in a high technology world.
I referred earlier to one of the very real problems of this country. It is a special problem, an accident of geography and history. A special problem is posed for Canada because many of the companies which are active here and many of the companies whose activities we require here send their research home to head offices. Unfortunately, we have to face this fact.
Many branch plants in Canada are miniature replicas of their parent companies. Their research and development programs often consist of very little more than adapting parental technology to Canadian tastes. As I said in Tilbury, Ontario, the other night, very often that means that we require that our rice crispies snap, crackle and pop in both official languages, but we do very little more to encourage real innovation in this country. No doubt the natural tendency-and 1 think this is a very important point to drive home-is to locate innovation at head offices. No doubt that tendency is encouraged by the fact that incentives for innovation in head office countries are much more dramatic than they are in Canada. That is the case with head offices in the United States and in other OECD countries, where most head offices are located. Competitive incentive by Canada could have some effect upon that trend, but the clear message for Canada is that this government, or the government we form, cannot continue on the path of pretending that a passive policy alone will be enough in the field of research and development.
We cannot afford to sit back and wait for proposals, because we have to face the fact that if there are proposals coming from many large corporations in this country for research and development, they do not come to the capital of this country.
They go to the head offices of those corporations in other countries. That is a reality we have to face. It is a reality which many of us are prepared to face because of the need we have for foreign investment. However, it is a very real and impor-
Research and Development
tant reality which must affect government policy, and it is a reason why there should be much more emphasis on innovation instead of less emphasis, as is the case with this government.
Given the drain to other countries where head offices are located, in our view the Government of Canada should go out and actively promote innovation in areas where Canada is best equipped to compete with the rest of the world and by companies which have a clear and unfettered commitment to Canada's interest. 1 want to make this point explicitly: that includes small Canadian companies.
I would like to turn the attention of the House for a moment to some of the special problems which are placed in the path of small Canadian companies which want to be active and innovative. One of the most serious is the simple burden of paper work. The paper work involved, for example, with the Enterprise Development Program is so overwhelming that mainly large companies apply because only large companies can hire the accountants, the lawyers, and the other experts who can weave their way through all that paper work. If the Government of Canada is serious about having the Enterprise Development Program serve the interests of small Canadian entrepreneurs, it should cut away that paper work and give them an equal chance at being helped in innovation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext:
The make or buy program was introduced some years ago, I believe by the present chairman of the National Capital Commission, another Liberal who has gone on to his reward at public expense. As the House will remember, that program was designed to reduce the proportion of Canadian research which was done in-house. While that make or buy program has had some success and has been of some use to the country, it has fallen far short of the success it could have registered. It was supposed to reduce the proportion of in-house research. When it was introduced, the proportion of in-house research in the country was 63 per cent in total. Today, after that program, it is 65 per cent. The reduction has been minus two. When that program was introduced, the intent was to drop the figure to somewhere in the neighbourhood of 30 per cent. Clearly the performance has fallen far short of the advertising, as happens so regularly in the activities of the government.
An active research policy, contrasted to a passive policy, would and should encourage development in areas of acknowledged Canadian expertise. We cannot run down the long, long list of those areas where Canadian expertise exists, but it is important to look at some of them. Clearly one is the communications industry, where some of our technology, particularly our satellite technology, is the most advanced in the world. Another clearly should concern ocean development through the Bedfords Institute, through others and through private firms, because as a country we have more accessible ocean floor than any other nation in the world. That holds untold opportunity for this country.

March 7, 1978
Research and Development
Obviously we should give much more research attention to agriculture. One of the things which shocks me about the government is the degree to which the interests of agriculture have been consistently shoved to the background. We have a minister who makes a good speech, but has little impact on the plans and the deliberations of his colleagues. That becomes evident in the plunge in farm incomes which has occurred during the life of this government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Also it becomes evident in the absolute failure of the government to give that kind of priority to agricultural research and development which that industry needs and, more important, which the nation needs.
Sometimes the government opposite tends to think of the food producers of Canada as some kind of group which it has to shoo away from time to time. The fact is that the food producers of Canada are the custodians of one of the most important resources this nation needs. In the long term, our capacity to grow and to produce food as a country, a capactiy which has few parallels elsewhere in the world, could be a resource as important to us as the petroleum which exists now. Unless we waste it, the food which can be harvested from our seas and fields is not a capacity which will run out as oil and other resources will run out. It is a capacity which becomes ever more important as world dietary habits change. We will not be able to take advantage of that resource for Canada unless there is a change in policy by the government.
First, we must make it profitable for Canadians to stay in agriculture, and second, we must give attention to research and development in order to take advantage of the application of technology to the great food resources of this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext:
I should like to dwell for a moment on the food industry and agriculture. Potentially we are one of the richest agricultural countries in the world. We are one of the richest food-producing countries, taking into account the great offshore resources. The government has failed dismally to plan for these resources and to put in effect fishing fleets which would take advantage of the resources that exist within our limits. Yet, in 1976, despite this wealth, 82.6 per cent of the Canadian market for agricultural products was served by imports. The Agricultural Institute of Canada has warned us that Canada's low investment in agricultural research "threatens Canada's position as a major world producer and supplier of food." Naturally we think that far more attention must be given to agricultural and general food research. In keeping with the principle of ensuring that more of that is done out of government, more and more of that research should be done in the fields, farms, and feedlots across the country. It should not be confined to urban or government laboratories.
Energy would appear to be an area where the world demand for innovation, the Canadian capacity to innovate, and Canadian resources could yield very, very high returns for this nation. I am anticipating remarks which will be made later in

the debate by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk). Finally, we must reverse the policy of this government which has had the effect of strangling medical research in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Athabasca will point out, joining with others knowledgeable in and concerned about medical research across the country, we cannot continue a situation where the policies of the Government of Canada drive away from this country the people who could be the seedbed and the focal point of our future medical research. The medical research policies which have been carried out by the government are not only hurting us today, they are hurting our capacity to prepare for the future. They are hurting that capacity in a way which perhaps cannot be remedied, unless the government turns around its policies and adopts some of the proposals the hon. member for Athabasca will be making later in the debate.
This is a country which calls forth imagination. Unlike many other countries in the world, Canada by its very nature encourages people to innovate. This is a country where people came from literally every corner in the world. They came here by choice. They came to build. In the early days of Canada our forefathers built with their hands, by their backs and with their brawn. In some parts of this country that is still necessary, but Canada lives in a different world now. We still require the determination to build which our ancestors showed. As I travel this country, I am convinced that Canadians still have that determination to build; but we must make it clear that our hands and our backs are not enough to build in the modern world. This is the age of technology. In the age of technology we require a capacity to innovate, a determination to experiment, and a determination to try new ventures, if we are to succeed as a country.
No one who travels across Canada will claim that we lack imagination or creativity as a country. Our investment in education ranks with the best in the world, as do our achievements in basic research in fields from medicine to nuclear energy. Creative talent is here in Canada. What is not here, and what must be here, is national leadership to match that creative potential with our economic objectives. speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the minister responsible for science and technology, 1 welcome the opportunity provided by the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) to speak on the state of research in Canada, and in particular on the state of industrial research and development. It is a matter of fundamental importance to the future well-being of this country and of concern to all of us.
Without a satisfactory level of industrial research and development, we cannot expect our economy to remain competitive in world markets, to create the new industrial opportunities which will create more jobs and raise our standard of living.
It is in recognition of these facts that the government has in recent years brought forward a number of measures to help and stimulate industrial R and D. The approach has been so designed as to assist all firms having an interest in research and development-whether they be large, small or medium sized.
The measure with the widest application is the 5 per cent to 10 per cent tax credit for research and development which was introduced a few months ago in last year's budget. It provides an immediate incentive of $35 million to $40 million to Canadian industry to increase expenditures on R and D. It has the advantage of leaving firms free to decide where and when they will invest, without direction by the government. This seems to me to be the most appropriate approach to take whenever possible.
The tax credit benefits mainly the larger and medium sized industrial establishments in Canada. On the other hand, smaller firms have tended to benefit from the contracting out policy under which new research for government is, whenever this is possible, carried out by the private sector. Under the policy, contracts placed with industry, which amounted to $18.9 million in 1973-74, the year in which the policy was put in place, rose to $86 million in 1976-77, and are expected to exceed $100 million this year. This amount will increase further as a result of the application of the policy to existing research activity within the government.
For R and D proposals originating with companies, the government has a number of programs of direct assistance. The most important of these is the enterprise development program which has a budget of $23 million. Other programs to meet specific needs are the NRC's technical information service, the industrial research assistance program, and the pilot industry laboratory program which are designed respectively to assist small firms with little or no research capacity of their own, to encourage growth of research capacity in companies,
Research and Development
and to facilitate the transfer of technology from NRC to industry.
In total, the government will spend $275 million to support industrial research in Canada in 1978-79. This amount excludes the revenue forgone as a result of the tax credit.
Industry has not been unresponsive to the need to increase Canada's R and D efforts and the measures taken by the government to encourage it. Its real rate of expenditures has risen during the seventies, but not to the extent desired. Thus, industry accounts for 34.9 per cent of all funds spent on R and D in 1977, compared to 32.4 per cent in 1971, and it performed 44.2 per cent of all research carried out in Canada compared to 41.4 per cent in 1971.
This redistribution of the national R and D effort is in the right direction. It remains evident, nevertheless, that by any reasonable standard of comparison, Canada's over-all R and D effort is too low compared to other industrial countries. For OECD countries as a whole, expenditures on R and D average 1.4 per cent of GNP. The corresponding figure for Canada is 1 per cent. A further analysis of these figures shows that while in Canada the private sector performs about 44 per cent of all R and D, in other OECD countries the percentage is something in the order of 50 per cent to 60 per cent.
It is fair to conclude from these comparisons that the shortfall in Canada's R and D effort is not mainly on the government side nor on that of the universities, but on the industrial side. Furthermore, it is clear that the shortfall is in the order of hundreds of millions of dollars. For instance, if a target for R and D of 1.5 per cent of GNP by 1983 were adopted, as suggested by the Senate committee, and if, furthermore, the industrial share of this total were to increase to 50 per cent, expenditures by industry on R and D would have to increase in constant dollars from an estimated $864.4 million in 1977 to $1.9 billion in 1983. The target proposed by the Leader of the Opposition would call for an over-all increase of $4.7 billion, or 17 per cent per annum. The task is formidable and cannot be accomplished without the full cooperation and co-ordination of all major R and D performers-the government, the universities and, most important, the industrial sector.
There are a number of general policy conclusions which can be drawn from this brief review of industrial R and D in Canada. First, Canada is seriously lagging behind other industrial countries in its R and D effort; second, while government and university research have a part to play in strengthening our R and D effort, the main responsibility and drive must come from the private sector itself; third, and more particularly, while there are no accepted criteria for establishing the amount of R and D which a country should perform, it appears that the shortfall in Canada must be measured in the hundreds rather than the tens of million dollars; fourth, the bulk of the R and D financing required by Canada must come from the private sector and not the government; fifth, the private sector must not only speak about the need for R and D, but show by its actions that it believes in investing in it; sixth, the government must continue to support R and D through not

March 7, 1978
Research and Development
a single measure but a variety of measures, such as a tax credit, whereby we can reach and assist all companies in the industrial sector; seventh, these measures should have a high leverage and call forth from the private sector several dollars for each dollar that the government commits.
These then are the general considerations which the government must take into account in the development of its industrial R and D policy. They are entirely consistent with the agreement at the first ministers' conference that "joint steps will be taken to improve tax incentives or credits for research and development". I am actively pursuing this matter with my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). One of our concerns about such a measure is that it should not result in a lower tax to firms now carrying out R and D without producing an appropriate increase in the level of R and D performed. It is possible to overcome this potential problem, but I would be more reassured if the private sector were to give a strong and clear indication that, if such a measure were taken, it would indeed increase its R and D expenditures.
Another factor that must be taken into account in considering the R and D situation in Canada is the high degree of foreign ownership. There is no doubt that Canada has benefited immensely from past foreign investment and the technology associated with it. But it has also created a number of structural problems which carry with them serious disadvantages. Most foreign firms tend to establish themselves in Canada to serve the Canadian market. In general, they rely on their parent for much of the R and D. To the extent they do perform R and D in Canada, it is frequently only the type required to adapt a product to the conditions of the Canadian market. The end product may be satisfactory to the consumer, but considerably less so in regard to the technological capacity of our industry. The cost of adaptation can be high and at times higher than the cost of doing the original R and D.
Many of the difficulties associated with this situation would be overcome if parent companies assigned R and D responsibilities to their subsidiaries hand in hand with the assignment of a product line for world-wide development.
Certainly, the R and D component of foreign investment in Canada must receive much more attention than in the past. FIRA, with the support of my colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), intends to give considerably greater weight to this factor in assessing the question of significant benefit so far as Canada is concerned.
The Leader of the Opposition referred to agriculture. 1 would just point out that the department of government with the largest expenditure on research and development is the Department of Agriculture. It spends more than $100 million a year on research and development. The largest operation it has is located in Alberta south of the riding of the Leader of the Opposition, in Lethbridge.
The government can also support the development of Canadian research and development capacity through its procurement policy. Admittedly this is an instrument which must

be used with a great deal of care. Nevertheless, it has in the past been used with successs as, for instance, in the case of national defence, space, and to a lesser extent so far, oceans. It is my intention to ensure that similar opportunities are fully exploited in the future. There are a number of areas which can be looked at, including transportation, energy, communications, and certain parts of the service sectors, all of which are technology and research and development intensive.
As I have already mentioned, the government has a number of grant programs designed to help small and medium-sized companies where cash constraints may be a serious short-term obstacle to investment in research and development. These programs need to be re-examined. Small businesses do have difficulties in getting access to new or up-to-date technology which they need to be fully competitive. There are great gains to be made by facilitating the access of these firms to this information.
Finally, I should say Mr. Speaker, that the vitality of any country's industrial research depends in the long run on basic research. The universities are uniquely capable of carrying out this task. Nevertheless, a far better bridge needs to be built between industrial and university research if the important problems affecting Canada are to be met effectively. This whole question of technology transfer was the subject of Report No. 28 published by the Science Council of Canada. It is for this reason that the government is urging universities to address more of their research to areas of national concern and to direct the results of their work, perhaps through such measures as innovation centres and changes in curriculi, to the economic and social enhancement of the lives of Canadians.
The Leader of the Opposition referred to the Kitimat pipeline. 1 found that interesting because, I suggest, there is a conflict within his own party. It is rather difficult to suck and blow at the same time. It seems to me it is either desirable to have tankers cruising up and down the west coast of British Columbia and coming into ports there, or it is not. I know the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) is very much opposed to this. The Leader of the Opposition should state his position clearly. Either he wants tankers coming into western Canadian ports, or he does not. If he does not, he must appreciate the decision that was taken not to proceed with the Kitimat pipeline at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think all Canadians would agree that one of the primary objectives of the people in this country should be the provision of jobs for all who are willing and able to work, yet in March, 1978, we have over one million people unemployed. The rate of unemployment is running at over 8 per cent of the labour force compared to the target of 3 per cent advocated by the Economic Council of Canada as late as 1964. It has been estimated an average of 475,000 school leavers will enter the labour market each year between now and 1985, yet in each of the last three years jobs have been found for just half that number entering the labour market.
March 7, 1978

In every industrialized country where the standard of living is high there is a very successful, very aggressive, and very efficient manufacturing industry, particularly in fields of high technology, that is, in every industrialized country except Canada. We in the New Democratic Party believe that Canada has a large enough population to maintain a successful manufacturing industry. After all, countries smaller than Canada such as Sweden, Switzerland, and Holland have built highly successful and sophisticated industries which compete on world markets.
Let us examine Canada's record, Mr. Speaker. In 1951 there were 1.3 million employees in manufacturing industries in Canada, but in 1976, 25 years later, only two million were involved in manufacturing-in other words a gain of only
700.000	jobs. To put it another way, in 1951 the manufacturing sector made up 25 per cent of the employment opportunities in Canada, but by 1976 the proportion had dropped to 20 per cent. Of the increase in jobs in this period, only 16 per cent came from the manufacturing sector and 86 per cent from the service sector. There was a net decline of 2 per cent of the total in utilities and construction.
These figures are taken from the sector papers tabled by the government at the first ministers' conference last month. They show that in primary textiles in 1973, the peak year, there were 86,000 employees, but three years later there were only 78,500, a decline of nearly 9 per cent. In clothing in 1973 there were about 125,000 employed, and now there are only 120,000; in electronics 67,917 were employed in 1966, but by 1976 only 64,000, a drop of almost 5 per cent; in electronic products
80.000	were employed in 1974, but by 1977 only 70,000 were employed, a drop of just under 13 per cent.
The problems were grave in every agency and every group I examined. One of the major difficulties is that our institutions-government agencies, universities, and even the private sector-are not contributing to research in the way that has been done in other industrialized countries. Both the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Buchanan) alluded to this.
I should like to put on the record an excerpt from a brief dealing with science in Canada which was submitted to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) by the Royal Society of Canada. The last paragraph on the first page reads as follows:
Although it was generally recognized that government support of industrial R & D was far too small in 1969, and although a substantial improvement was made in 1970, by 1975 it had decreased, when considered as a fraction of the GNP, to as little as 87 per cent of that in 1969; in terms of the fraction of federal budgetary expenditures it had fallen to 68 per cent. To make matters worse, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commence has abolished its IRDIA program (for which the 1974-75 expenditures were $32 million) and has cut back its PAIT program. These programs are of vital importance to high-technology industries and these actions will seriously hamper the attempts of these industries to improve their foreign markets and increase their productivity.
It has been calculated that the proportion of the gross national product spent by the federal government for basic research through the two main funding agencies, the National Research Council and the Medical Research Council, has been
Research and Development
steadily decreasing since 1969. Then it was a mere 0.10, in other words, one tenth of one per cent of the gross national product. By 1976 it was an appalling 0.07 per cent. By contrast, Belgium spent 0.3 per cent; Germany 0.3 per cent; France 0.4 per cent; Japan 0.4 per cent, and The Netherlands 0.6 per cent of their gross national product. In other words, Canada spent about one quarter of the average support level of these west European countries and Japan.
Or, to put it another way, in 1974 Canada's increase over the 1969 support level was about 8 to 10 per cent, whereas that of West Germany was 150 per cent, France 100 per cent, United Kingdom 60 per cent, and the United States 50 per cent. Clearly, unlike Canada, these countries recognized that their basic research capability provides the underpinning for future technological development which promotes a strong secondary manufacturing section with its high growth of employment opportunities.
As I have indicated, the Leader of the Opposition and the Minister of State for Science and Technology have dwelt on the failure of Canada to meet the needs of this country in the fields of research and development. But both of them wish us to continue to depend on the private sector of our economy by providing it with more tax incentives. This type of approach has failed in the past and there is little reason to expect a real change in the future. The reasons why it has failed should be obvious. It has failed because to a large extent our basic industry is in the resource extraction area, which requires a minimum of research and development. For example, in 1969 among the 14 nations belonging to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, Canada has the second lowest percentage of workers in the manufacturing area-23 per cent; with Ireland being the lowest-20 per cent. By comparison, the percentage in West Germany was 38 per cent, in the United Kingdom 36 per cent, and the United States 34 per cent.
As well, Canada has the highest degree of foreign ownership and control of its industry among the OECD countries. In most of these multinational companies, of which Canada has such a proliferation, a major part of their research and development takes place in the head office country. For example, Ford of Canada is a major industrial firm in Canada, yet Ford carries out no research and development in Canada and employs not one science Ph.D. in all of its Canadian operations.
We have seen in the last few years as the world economy has moved into its present state of recession that only a small amount of research and development was carried on by Canadian corporations. Let us face the fact that the bulk of Canadian research and development is carried on in most countries by large corporations. But because such a large percentage of Canadian industries, and particularly of our manufacturing industries, is composed of mere branch plants of multinational corporations, we have had very substantial cutbacks in the meagre research and development carried on by those corporations.

March 7, 1978
Research and Development
A classic example, Mr. Speaker, which can be repeated many times, is what happened to the RCA research facilities in the Montreal area. As the corporation headquarters, mainly in the United States, felt the fall off in business, they moved the entire RCA research facilities which employed hundreds of people in the Montreal area back to the United States.
I know that I am not exaggerating the difficulties. In a study prepared by the Science Council entitled "Uncertain Prospects-Canadian Manufacturing Industry, 1971-1977" they say in part, and I quote from page 2 of their report:
In 1971 the Science Council was especially concerned about the viability and survival of medium and high technology industries. In 1977 there are real fears about the prognosis for Canadian manufacturing as a whole.
In other words, the Science Council is worried about our whole manufacturing industry. It goes on to say on the same page:
It is apparent that the technological capability of Canadian industry has not improved. It has in fact deteriorated. Exports of technology-intensive goods have fallen in relative terms, and many of the industries which produce them are unable to meet foreign competition in the domestic market. Job opportunities for scientists, engineers, M.B.A.s, executives, and other specialists are scarce or non-existent. .. This year's university graduates face the most dismal job prospects of the last forty years. Human resources, which have been created at great cost, are being squandered.
Having spent 25 years developing an educational system in which our universities can compete in quality with universities the world over, we now find ourselves in a situation in which we are turning out something in the neighbourhood of 2,500 Ph.D.'s a year, for most of whom there are really no jobs in Canadian industry, Canadian universities, or in Canadian governments. This is the situation, Mr. Speaker. Neither the Leader of the Opposition nor the Minister of State for Science and Technology faced up to this situation. They did not face up to it because they refused to face up to the fact that our industry is to an overwhelming extent controlled by multinational corporations. Its policies are devised not in Canada but in other countries and those multinational corporations are under the constant pressure of the governments and the peoples of the countries in which their headquarters are located.
How can Canadian citizens and the Canadian government expect multinational corporations to act any differently when we live so close to the heartland of the industrial population of the United States? We know of the situation in which they are. We know they are facing unemployment at rates almost as high as those in Canada. Why should we be surprised if United States corporations and U.S. workers and unions are now calling on the American government to protect the jobs and well-being of the people of that country?
We find it almost impossible to deal with that situation. We are caught in the same trap as all of the other countries in the industrialized world because of the recession which has increased unemployment to a height we have not experienced since the end of World War II. To a large extent the decisions are not made by Canadian governments, corporations or workers, but by the multinational corporations. I do not say that in criticism of them. If there is to be criticism, it should be criticism of the Canadian governments and the Canadian
[Mr. Orlikow.J
people who elected those governments which, over the years, have failed to face up to the problems arising out of the result of this situation.
Over the years we have encouraged the development of our resource base industry. We have failed to realize, even today, that those industries are to a large extent capital intensive rather than labour intensive. Compared with our manufacturing industries, they do not employ many people. We have failed to realize that those industries face competition from other countries. A classic example is what happened at Sudbury.
At the same time that INCO, one of our largest corporations, was operating plants in Canada, employing Canadian workers and making profits in Canada, it was using those profits and the know-how it learned in Canada to develop competing sources in Indonesia and Guatemala. I do not blame INCO. It is responsible to its shareholders. It did what it thought it should do for its shareholders. However, that was not at all in the best interests of the Canadian people.
If we are to use the full potential of Canadians and have full employment, we must change our policies. We should concentrate more of our efforts on the manufacturing industry rather than the resource industry. We must concentrate on high technology and modern industries.
Canadian people are well educated. We have the research facilities, if we want to use them, to compete with other countries. Our manufacturing industries must be concentrated. We must break the stranglehold of the multi-nationals. Our efforts must be concentrated on developing Canadian owned and operated corporations which will make their own decisions and which will try to meet the needs of the Canadian people. That can be done by greater emphasis on planning and direction by the government, not only of its resources, facilities, and the use of Canadian universities, but by bringing Canadian industries into those fields that will meet the needs of the Canadian people.
We support in general the criticisms made by the Leader of the Opposition in today's motion and support most of the provisions in the motion he proposed on behalf of the official opposition. However, we believe there is a serious lack in that motion. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the motion be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a semi-colon and by adding thereafter a new paragraph (6) to read as follows:
"(6) require Canadian subsidiaries of foreign-based corporations to devote a
specified portion to Canadian-based research and development expenditures,
in order to break the branch-plant nature of our manufacturing industry."

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased, on this allotted day, to take part in a discussion on a topic of special concern to all Canadians, namely our economy. Today,
March 7, 1978

serious problems such as unemployment have been dwelt upon and stressed. It was pointed out that we now have over a million unemployed in Canada. It was also pointed out, and rightly so, that a high number of our large, medium and small businesses are underemployed, that they do not produce as efficiently as they could. Now, Mr. Speaker, those are problems we must face today, and which could have largely been avoided, to my mind, if most of the recommendations that were made had been implemented fairly quickly.
The Senate Special Committee on Science Policy, set up in 1970, looked into all aspects of the science policy in Canada. They published a three-volume report explaining at length what problems we have in Canada and what would happen if we did not consider immediate reforms in those fields.
Unfortunately, the government put off implementing those recommendations. It did appoint a minister with some responsibilities in the early '70s, a few responsibilities, not too great, with the result that during the summer of 1975, the Senate had to resume its studies and publish a fourth volume to complete its study. As a result of that second inquiry, the existence of great concern came to light, and the chairman of the committee, Senator Lamontagne, revealed in November of 1977, that in real terms there had been no progress since 1970 with regard to the level and distribution of national and government effort in the field of scientific research and development.
Indeed, the Senate committee which carried out special studies in this area practically blamed the federal government for not doing anything tangible or worthwhile to solve this problem. I would like to take the opportunity of this debate to show that it is essential to have a strong Canadian economy and intensify the employment policy that the government establish a long term scientific policy; as everyone knows, strong research potential is essential to Canada's progress. That potential has yet to be developed to an acceptable level.
It would even appear that the present level of research is threatened due to a lack of young scientists involved in basic research which results in an average aging of researchers without any possibility of replacement. This problem will reach its crucial point in the 1990's and probably even before the 1990's. And one of the reasons of this lack of interest of young scientists for research is surely the freeze on grants that was imposed in December 1975 and which mainly affects university researchers.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, in early November 1977, at the Social Credit Party of Canada convention which was held in Drum-mondville in the province of Quebec the members who were attending that convention passed a resolution dealing with long term scientific policies, and with the Chair's permission, I would like to read that resolution into the record as follows:
Research and Development
That a government headed by the Social Credit Party of Canada undertake to reinvigorate (university) private research by establishing at least a five year scientific policy along the following three basic principles: (1) the need for an adequate budget; (2) the urgence of establishing a three to nine year long term Canadian scientific policy; and (3) the presence of a representative of the research community on grant committees.
We believe, Mr. Speaker that it is very important to have a representative of the research community on a grant committee for university researchers. Furthermore, another thing we fear is that the few researchers we have in Canada might not want to stay because long term employment opportunities are nearly inexistent in this country. So this causes them to go and look somewhere else for a steady job and results in Canada being a sort of bank of researchers for other countries.
Mr. Speaker, Canada is now investing only 80 per cent of what Italy invests in research and development. Yet Italy ranks eighth among the rich countries. It invests 1.1 per cent of its national product, and we invest 0.8 per cent. I have here a table for the year 1975 of OECD member countries. We are told that the United States spent 2.3 per cent of their gross national product on scientific research; the United Kingdom, 2.5 per cent; West Germany, 2.4 per cent; Holland, 2 per cent; Japan, 1.8 per cent; Sweden, 1.6 per cent; France, 1.5 per cent and Italy, 1.1 per cent, and Canada came in ninth and last with 0.9 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, it amounts to saying that our efforts were surely not very considerable and for a country like Canada I think that in the field of scientific and technological research we could have accomplished for many years a lot more than we have done till now. Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of 1976, government investments fell to less than 0.5 per cent of the gross national product and only 0.1 per cent has been assigned to research carried in the universities and 0.1 per cent to industrial research the two most productive sectors for such spendings. The United States invest 2.3 per cent of their gross national product into research. This is why we are dependent on them as well as on the multinationals. They are the ones who have that research work done for us. They are the ones who can offer secure and long term employment opportunities for scientists.
Mr. Speaker, the issue of the non-availability of objective information is so fundamental to the solution of our problems in the field of evergy policies that it has been raised by a Liberal minister, the Hon. Donald S. Macdonald in 1974 in an interview with the representatives of the magazine Oil Week, and I quote: "One of the difficulties facing the Canadian government is that it is almost completely dependent on the multinationals for its sources of information". This is why, Mr. Speaker, it is absolutely necessary that the government react right now and see to it that the monies allocated to research and to development reach 2.5 per cent of the gross national product by 1985 at the latest, in order to restore in that manner a strong economy and to increase the employment opportunities already existing in that field.
3532

March 7, 1978
Research and Development
The minister mentioned that tax credits have been granted to Canadian businesses and companies. As for me, I think that the large businesses, these national corporations can well manage by themselves but the small or medium size business finds itself in a different position. Small or medium size businesses have little opportunities to undertake scientific research even if they are entitled to tax credits. This is why other institutions such as universities for instance are put in charge of scientific research work and have to constitute data banks which are made available to small and medium size businesses. In my opinion such is the way, Mr. Speaker, whereby we will meet the needs of these businesses for they do not have non the means to make this research even if the government is to grant them tax credits.
Mr. Speaker, up to now the planning of natural resources such as energy has been left to multinationals whose only purpose is not the common good but profits made even at the risk of ruining the people in years to come. I think we should increase our research, through universities, in the field of renewable energy and it is on that point that 1 want to conclude my comments this afternoon. In connection with multinationals, especially those involved in the development of energy resources, I think they are doing their best. Those resources are not renewable, but very little has been done to develop resources such as solar energy.
Until recently, only 0.4 per cent of the amounts allocated by the government was spent on research in solar energy, wind energy, renewable energy, whereas these are the very fields, Mr. Speaker, where heavy investments should have been made several years ago. Thus Canadians would not be running scared, constantly hearing as they do that in a few years we may lack energy for heating, for manufacturing consumer goods, for transporting them or for transporting ourselves.
Mr. Speaker, I believe one of our priorities should be to intensify research in renewable energy, and our universities, provided we grant them the necessary funding, can capture the interest of the young in that field, and ensure that we do not face a lack of researchers in a few years, because they will then be too old and unable to produce, and because we will not have foreseen the necessary replacements to carry on. Mr. Speaker, I think the motion we are debating today is an extremely important one, which should encourage the government to implement reforms which have been recommended mainly by the Senate committee, the universities and other organizations which have offered to co-operate with the government to improve this situation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in a rapidly changing technology oriented world research and development are the key to the future. Without research and development we will lose in international competition to competing countries and lose our place as an industrialized nation.
[Mr. Laprise.l
Clearly, research and development are the great multiplier that enables Canadians to maintain and improve their high standard of living by producing goods in our industrial sector for sale in Canada and abroad at competitive prices, and putting more Canadians to work at good jobs to produce those goods. There is a clear need for a strategy to stimulate significantly our innovative research and development capacity in those industries in which we have the potential for a comparative trade advantage.
Canada has had some excellent success in pure research science but appears to be weak in applied scientific research.
It is not easy to determine the effect of the government's policies in achieving Canada's scientific goals because, as the latest report of the Senate committee on science policy indicates, Canada's stated policy objectives have not always been those it has implemented. In promoting industrial development the government would financially assist universities to train scientists and engineers while building its own laboratories where the bulk of the nation's research would be conducted. Industry would then be provided with the results of this scientific research to solve its problems and to manufacture new products as technology advanced.
This concept seems to prevail still although its wisdom is called into question when we consider the 30 per cent decline in research and development since 1970, last year's $12 billion deficit in end product trade, and the capture of almost one third of all domestic sales by imported goods.
As a provider of jobs, Canada's manufacturing industry has eroded to the point where today it accounts for only 19 per cent of the nation's work force as against 25 per cent in 1950. Indeed, without the auto pact, defence production sharing, and similar bilateral arrangements with the United States, Canada would have few exports of manufactured goods.
Our lack of technological innovation, the problems of inadequate industrial research, and difficulties in transferring technology from government laboratories to meaningful functions in our manufacturing industries are major factors contributing to our present economic stagnation. Canadians have demonstrated the ability to replace our absolete second-hand technology with meaningful research which can make us world leaders in selected manufacturing areas. Examples of Canadian industrial success exist, but they must be built upon and multiplied. To do this, research and development must be encouraged through the development of coherent national policies aimed at enhancing our industrial base.
In October of 1977 the special committee of the Senate on science policy published its fourth and last report in its series on science policy for Canada entitled "Progress and Unfinished Business". The report concludes that much time has been wasted and that only now are some of the recommendations of several years ago being put into practice.
The Ministry of State for Science and Technology was expected to become the pivot around which science policy decisions would be made, but in practice it has become a mere service agency assisting other departments in the preparation
March 7, 1978

of their own particular scientific programs. If the Ministry of State for Science and Technology is to have an important role and make a major contribution to maintaining and expanding the standard of living enjoyed by Canadians, it will require the leadership and internal stability which can be achieved only with a full time minister through a continuity of management personnel and a minimum of reorganization. In six years MOSST has had five different ministers and three different deputy ministers. That can hardly be called stability. No wonder the Science and Engineering Council established by Bill C-26 last July has never been appointed, and neither has its chairman nor any of its members.
This same haphazard, lackadaisical approach toward science is reflected in the failure of the government to appoint the chairman of the Medical Research Council since that position became vacant last June.
No wonder the budget for the Medical Research Council in the current estimates is increased by only 5.7 per cent, which does not even keep pace with the decline in purchasing power of the dollar.
The National Research Council estimates, on the other hand, show an apparent increase of 11 per cent, and this may look good in terms of the consumer price index. The CPI measures the percentage change over time in the price of a constant basket of goods and services normally purchased by the average Canadian family in the average Canadian city. These are not, however, the same goods and services which Canadian scientists must purchase in order to do research in this country.
The Medical Research Council and the National Research Council have each developed a specialized cost index to calculate the true impact of inflation in their areas of interest. Both indices show that the erosion of the science dollar by inflation over the past seven years has been much greater than the increase in the Consumer Price Index.
For the period 1969-1976 the difference between the Consumer Price Index and the National Research Council science cost index was 28.8 per cent or, in terms of 1969-1976 constant dollars, this represented an extra loss of $23.5 million in the purchasing power of NRC supported non-governmental research.
In view of this very large discrepancy in the results shown by the specialized science deflaters on the one hand and the Consumer Price Index on the other, the government should be prepared to use a cost index which would accurately measure the effects of inflation when determining the size of granting budgets allocated for research. This returns us again to the question of how to measure the impact of government policies on Canada's scientific effort.
I suggest that the best method, and the one most commonly used, is to relate the sum of all research in private and public sectors to a fraction of the gross national product and compare it with other industrialized countries. This would compensate for price fluctuation related to inflation and would also reflect population and economic dimensions.
Research and Development
The conclusions in terms of Canada's contribution are not very good. Canada does not spend as much relatively on research and development as do competing industrialized countries. In fact, Canada today spends less than half as much of its gross national product on research and development as do the United States, the United Kingdom and West Germany.

speechtext:
Less than Japan too. I thank the hon. member. In moving to the position where we spend 2.5 per cent of our gross national product we shall be approaching the fraction now spent in those other industrialized countries I have just mentioned.
Our performance to date is not good, and it is getting worse. What are the results? Today imports serve nearly 30 per cent of the Canadian market for manufactured goods, 88 per cent of the Canadian market for computer and office equipment, and 60 per cent of the Canadian market for consumer electronic products. Considering the decline in the value of the dollar on international markets, we can clearly see the terrific price Canadians will soon be paying for the failure of this government to stimulate Canadian industry to keep abreast of innovations in the field of research and development.
If this record were not bad enough, the tragedy is that 83 per cent of the Canadian domestic market for farm machinery is supplied by imported goods. Unless this situation is completely turned around, our hard pressed farmers will soon be dealt another cruel and severe economic blow. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) says this is good for them!
Research must be encouraged to the maximum, especially applied research. A significant increase in the research and development tax credit is imperative, and we must extend the tax credit system to provide special incentives for new employment in industrial research, design and development. These incentives must be of a continuing nature, with a definite time commitment given to industry to give it confidence that the government is convinced of the importance of research and development as an essential base for economic advancement. The government should also encourage the transfer of scientific knowledge and technology in a co-operative effort between universities, government, and industries. There are tremendous opportunities for scientific research and development to be encouraged in areas of regional disparity in Canada. I am thinking of fisheries, forestry, food processing, oceanography, and specialized fields. For example, in the area of fisheries, experimentation is warranted in fish culture and breeding, fish ranching, fish processing, fishing technique, apparatus development, fish boat construction and equipment. A new first could be achieved in seaweed culture on which very little has so far been done in North America.
In forestry I think in terms of silviculture, parasite control, and wood processing. In food processing, effective research can
