March 7, 1978
Research and Development
be done in fish and farm products. In oceanography, tidal studies as an outgrowth of the Fundy project are a natural area for development in the Atlantic provinces. The Bedford Institute of Oceanography in Halifax is the best in the world and is not adequately supported by this government.
We can expand research and development associated with using waste hot water from thermal and nuclear plants for fish growing, seaweed culture, farming and greenhouse cultivation. In this respect we have a potential to grow vegetables which we now import.
In renewable energy we have unlimited opportunities for research and development, not just in solar energy and wind energy, but also including peat moss, methanol, and wood as a fuel. We can explore even the possibilities of accelerating present research into the use of hydrogen as an energy fuel and developing it with the electric energy generated by tidal action used as a catalyst in our oceans.
Our universities have offered us a tremendous opportunity to have excellent research performed, while at the same time stimulating the teaching and learning potential of our universities and assisting in the development of the badly needed young scientists who can take their places in the private sector of our economy, after it is stimulated by the next government with a meaningful industrial strategy.
I should like to share with hon. members some relevant comments made by Dr. Thomas Vanderslice at the Financial Post conference held in Ottawa on January 25, 1978. He said the following:
The underlying paradox in all of these trends today is the accumulating evidence that there is a high and positive correlation between technology and the things we need: jobs, improved productivity, resistance to inflation and economic growth.
To get a fix on this, we asked data resources to make an analysis of output, employment and price behaviour in high and low technology industries in the United States over a 25-year period.
We found that high technology industries grew almost three times as fast.
The same is true for productivity, output per employee in high technology industries was double that of the low.
The favourable labour productivity is mirrored in the price record: with high technologies much more resistant to inflation.
An even more significant finding is that the gains in output per worker were not at the expense of employment. Employment in high technology industries in the United States has been growing almost nine times as fast as in the low.
The same kind of favourable ratios prevail in terms of international trade. The positive contribution of "high technology" products is up to a plus of over $25 billion a year.
While the United States trade balance in products with "low" technical content is down from break-even in 1960 to a $16 billion deficit.
Thus, our experience clearly indicates that high technology industries have outperformed intermediate and low technology industries in terms of real growth, productivity, less price inflation, and higher employment. From 1950 to 1974, output per man-hour rose at a 4 per cent annual pace in sectors devoting an above average share of income to research and development. This is better than twice the productivity growth achieved by industries with lower than average commitments to new technology.
Ours is a young country, rich in resources, with a shining promise for tomorrow. All that is necessary to bring it about is a new attitude and constructive new policies, such as the ones just enunciated a few moments ago by my leader. My leader

has demonstrated that he is the best leader of any political party in Canada today, and that he has the vision, determination, and energy to lead this nation out of the economic mess in which it now finds itself.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to have an opportunity to participate in this debate concerning research and development. 1 do not think anyone doubts the importance of research and development as part of an economic strategy in Canada to help us make a transition to more technically efficient industry. We know that research
March 7, 1978

and development are an essential element in any policy for a rapid return to full employment based on expansion of the manufacturing and resource sectors. In some parts of industry, these sectors are in a cul-de-sac of technological dependency, which is a term used by the Science Council of Canada. This dependency refers to a weak capacity, to weak opportunities and to weak incentives for research and development in Canada, thus not helping us to break out of that situation of dependency into a more technically efficient base for the future.
Research and development are a key element in securing for Canadian industry a higher share of the world market and a higher share of the domestic market, which is rapidly being occupied by imports. Research and development turn the key to better performance and a more competitive Canadian industry. Thus, none of us can doubt their importance.
The resolution before the House emphasizes the tax environment as an encouragement to research and development. I do not think a great deal of argument can be found with the proposals in the resolution, so far as they go. They really go only so far as the tax system can go to assist greater research and development activity in Canada. I will attempt to present an argument to my colleagues in the House indicating that a wider policy and support framework than taxation is required. Even improved tax incentives will not prove adequate. Some reasons for this have already been mentioned. For example, the structure of Canadian industry is so highly foreign-owned that most research and development is done outside the country and transferred into it.
While the magnitude of tax incentive is important, they will not do the entire job. However, so far as the tax environment goes, from my examination of the subject I believe the tax credit for investment in research and development should be increased significantly. At present it stands at 10 per cent in the Atlantic area and the Gaspe. It is IVi per cent in other designated regions. It is 5 per cent in the faster growth regions of the country. Five per cent is not enough. While we should retain regional differentiation, we should move up to at least 15 per cent, with a low point of at least 10 per cent. Discussing these percentages, however, is not perhaps as useful as saying that we should put ourselves on an equivalent basis with the investment tax credit in the United States.
Our investment tax credit of, say, 10 per cent works like this: if an investment is on a scale of $10 million, the investment tax credit is $1 million applied to that. This sounds like a very powerful incentive, but when you consider that it becomes taxable in the hands of the receiver and that perhaps 46 per cent of it is taxed back, it has lost a good deal of its punch. When you consider also that it is deducted from the capital cost in our example of $10 million, and one begins the capital cost allowances at the $9 million level, again it has lost some of its impact, which it does notloseinthecaseofourcompetitorsin the United States. So I think the principle should be that in the research and development tax environment we should be at
Research and Development
least as competitive as are our U.S. companies. The tax credit should be adjusted upward to achieve this goal.
I should like to refer also to the tariff environment because it is one of the important horizontal type policies under which all our companies operate. We are going through the GATT negotiations in Geneva in which most of the countries in the world are engaged, and if various formulae changes come through, there will be significant across the board reductions in tariffs, amounting to perhaps more than 40 per cent. We in Canada would have to ensure that we do not go only for an across the board tariff reduction but that we negotiate the average 40 per cent or so in terms of an industrial strategy which has singled out some industries for maintained tariff protection, while we proceed through a transitional period to a more competitive strength for them. That transition will require a host of policies in addition to taxes and tariff.
We should be highly selective, having made some choices of the industries with the promise of a future in this country. We know in general where they are. They are in telecommunications; they are in the ocean industries where we must have enormous potential advantages; they are in transport technology where we have enormous spaces to cover at low cost and therefore we must do the R and D necessary to ensure that low cost. We have advantages in petrochemicals where we should be looking at the average tariff reductions to maintain positions in the key exposed but potentially favourable sectors and to compensate with lower tariffs where we can face world competition because of world scale production and other advantages. The same holds true in the plastics industry, and 1 could also mention machinery, pharmaceuticals, and the construction industry, to continue the list of examples. However, the main point is that in tariff structures, as in tax structures, we should have R and D incentives in mind in certain industries.
I said I wanted to argue for a wider framework of policy than the tax suggestions indicated in the resolution in front of us, and I will do that by noting that in the forefront of our concerns now is the structure of the Canadian industrial economy. The structure of the economy need not be a difficult concept for us. Such items as I will mention enter into the question of the appropriate Canadian economic structure to face into the new world environment in which we find ourselves. Part of that new world environment is the oncoming of the Third World with industrial products of quality. We will have to face their competition doubly because we have given them preferred low tariffs. How can we ensure that Canadian industry will face that stiff new competition if we do not help reorganize its structure and reshape it?
1 will mention some of the elements which I think fit into that kind of restructuring of our basic industrial plant. First, we should adopt policies which encourage a larger scale in many industrial sectors so that they can achieve the gains from specialization and so that they have a base of production big enough to support the huge R and D expenditures that are necessary today.

March 7, 1978
Research and Development
When we consider, for example, that Northern Telecom- which is perhaps our outstanding example of R and D work in Canada-had to spend some $70 million to bring in its latest piece of hardware for the world market, an advanced kind of switching equipment for telephone systems. It remains a leader in the world but the R and D base had to be $70 million. Surely that requires a large scale company. There will be hundreds of suppliers of equipment to Northern Telecom across Canada which will be able to produce and supply components for that piece of advanced technology developed through Canadian research and innovation. They are dependent on these big core companies being so large and specialized that they can carry the weight of $70 million. We must therefore have the policies that will support that kind of scale. Taxes alone will not assure us that. That means that our competition Act and other policies must support enterprise structures capable of specialization and scale of operations.
Second, it means that the whole market in Canada must be collected, as it were, or aggregated so that key companies have a home base and a somewhat assured market. Tariffs are one form of giving some assurance, but today they cannot be taken too far. Another form of assuring the home market is procurement policies of governments. Should our hydro systems purchase Canadian technology or should they go to Switzerland, Britain, Japan or Germany? If we are serious about aggregating the market to give a home base for our own companies, then we must consider the industrial strategy advantage of procurement policies which pull the market together. While ensuring that these are good products-and there is no question in anybody's mind that we have a leading technology in heavy electrical equipment-we need to help companies come together in consortia without falling afoul of the competition act, if we are interested in the industrial implications of employment and income in Canada, faced as the country is with new problems.
For example, let us consider the amalgamation which took place of Canadian General Electric, General Steel Wares, and Westinghouse to put together a large enough company to manufacture many lines of electrical goods, and also the consortium represented by Petrosar in Sarnia where four very large Canadian companies were not large enough individually to build a polyethylene plant on a world scale, but the four together, assisted by government encouragement, are big enough and are now in the final stages of a technology and an enterprise that will supply Canada with resins which go into the plastics industry. That leads one to look at intermediate manufacturing stages.
What about the security of the plastics industry in Canada? Thirty per cent of that market is occupied by imports, an unusually high share in terms of western countries. Why do we have a low occupation of our own market with all of these new polyethylene and resins coming into play? What can we do to ensure R and D in the plastics industry so that it will play a full role in processing the products of the petrochemical industry? Let me illustrate. Auto parts will use a lot more plastic. There are about 200 pounds of plastics in an automobile today.

In five years' time even smaller automobiles will use 600 pounds of plastics. Are we going to produce them? Will we have the R and D to do it, and will we have the other industrial policies to encourage the plastics industry to establish in Canada?
There are certain other major projects, such as the liquid natural gas project which could bring natural gas from the Arctic islands to the east coast. That major project approach embraces many technologies and would require research and development in tankers, transportation systems, liquifaction systems, electronic and processing equipment, control equipment, and so on. We need co-ordinated policies in order to put all these things together. I mention them to illustrate that more than taxes is required to form the incentive for research and development. The structure of the economy and the way we co-ordinate policies count for much. Without research and development we are not likely to pull ourselves out of our present situation.
I will quickly mention venture capital corporations and tax incentives to encourage individuals and institutions to invest in them, particularly in small and medium industries where much innovation is found. These industries need venture capital to carry them through all stages from research and development to the production of prototypes, testing of the market and getting into exports. We need policies much broader than tax policies to assist small and medium industries to come together, perhaps in research consortia and to find venture capital so that they can enter the market successfully. If we are serious about research and development we will have to do these things.
Something else we must do is to stimulate the growth of Canadian multinational companies. Our experience is that most multinationals-and we have their subsidiaries in this country-do their research and development at head office. These subsidiaries receive the technology after it has been developed and the parent company has made the product innovation and established the world market. This is no longer good enough. We must help Canadian companies become multinationals so that they will have the wide base that will enable them to afford research and development and produce goods that they can sell around the world.
1 want now to come to my final remarks, Mr. Speaker, and move from the question of industrial structure to the government's approach to new policies. In the four months preceding the first ministers' conference the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) dealt personally with the industrial strategy issue in Canada. I think that as a result the prospects for the future look good. The first ministers in their February meeting agreed that they would examine the Canadian economy sector by sector-they would examine the problems of the pulp and paper sector and what could be done there, the machinery sector, the furniture sector, plastics, pharmaceuticals, automobiles and so on. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) pointed out, the automobile industry is a hollow
March 7, 1978

industry in Canada. There is no research and development done here.
Why not?

That is a good question. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) dealt only with taxes, which are important but are not the total problem.
The sector approach will mean that both levels of government and both sides of industry, labour and management, will look at the same facts and set objectives for an industry. These working groups may discuss the share of the home market an industry should seek and the share of the export market it should seek and what this would require in productivity gains or what it would require in terms of labour-management adversary relationships or greater collaboration-what it would mean in terms of federal tax policy, provincial tax policy and federal and provincial incentives. All this will be examined by working groups sector by sector. 1 think this is perhaps the most hopeful sign in some time of help to improve the performance of the Canadian economy in its most important sectors.
The second approach required is that the federal government put its own house in order with respect to the many departments in the economic policy field. Should the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce take the lead-the Department of Employment and Immigration, the Department of Finance, or of science and technology and so forth? There must be greater co-ordination.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, we must review the parent-subsidiary relationship in industrial sectors. Some parent companies do all the research and pass the technology on; some Canadian subsidiaries such as Canadian General Electric do some research and supply it to the rest of the world as is the case in heavy electrical turbines. Other subsidiary companies have a free hand, and companies such as Hewlett-Packard develop laboratories in Canada with their own engineering staff. Any product they develop they can take anywhere in the world. That is the kind of relationship we must strive for in an industrial policy, so that subsidiaries can be innovative and can do their own research and development. If there is not that relationship with the parent company, all the tax changes we can devise will not bring about greater research and development.
1 will conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that tax measures are fine but they only go part way. This is a bigger question, however. We need action programs and policies in order to devise industrial strategies sector by sector and bring research and development into full bloom in Canada.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, having listened to the Minister of Public Works and Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Buchanan), and to the hon. member who just resumed his seat, I am convinced that the government still has not recognized the important role that
Research and Development
investment in research and development can play in the economic growth of this country.
I welcome the opportunity to speak in this debate today and I want to deal largely with the area of medical research since it has also been neglected by this government. It seems to me that an accelerating erosion has been taking place in this area, to the point of utter destitution. I am very sorry that the minister who opened the debate for the government failed to answer questions which people across the country are asking about the future of research, and particularly about the future of medical research in Canada.
Evidence can be found everywhere in the country that the policies of this Liberal administration have demoralized and discouraged the research community to the nth degree and have given rise to the threat of massive unemployment in that community.
I suppose, to put it in perspective, one should analyze the basis of Liberal policy, or rather the lack of policy. Careful examination of their behaviour in the area of research reveals two very significant factors. First, the government does not believe that research has to be done in this country if you can get it from other countries free of charge by reading their scientific journals. That is one of the basic premises upon which the Liberal government's science policy has been based over the life of the current Liberal administration.
Another premise on which they seem to be basing their science policy, or lack of it, is that money put into research is just another expenditure. It is just like paying the light bill or the gas bill at the end of the month. That is a horrible misconception of research. Anyone who has thought about this matter for any period of time quickly comes to the realization that money put into research is one of the best investments any country, any company, or anyone can make.
Hear, hear!

If we look at some of the documented evidence that has been provided to members of this House we can easily find examples showing expenditures on research or investments which bring huge returns. I would like to cite two examples. The first is the dollar savings because of decreased mortality, morbidity, loss of earnings, and institutionalization following the development of the polio vaccine in the United States. If we compare the cost of the various factors which I have just mentioned prior to the use of polio vaccine to the cost of the development and administration of a polio vaccine program, we can see quite clearly that the costs prior to the vaccine were $6.7 billion. During the same period, the research costs and the administration of the program were $653 million. That is a ratio of return on investment of very close to 100 to one.
We can look at another area for which calculations have been made, that of immunology. The cost benefit analyses which have been done relating to immunology show the ratio of savings is again 100 to one. That is not to say all research

March 7, 1978
Research and Development
done results in a return in permanently reduced health care costs of 100 to one. But if you tidy it all up the ratio perhaps for the over-all field is in the range of 10 to one or 20 to one.
Any government which stands before this House and tells the country we are in a time of restraint and that we must save money by cutting expenditure on health research is simply being stupid. I am sorry I have to use that word but I cannot think of a more fitting term to apply to the kind of approach this government has been following.
I want to point out, Mr. Speaker, evidence of the crime. 1 consider the policies of this government a crime. 1 want to cite a number of examples which can only open one's eyes more to the situation that has resulted. Not only in the long run but even in the short run all of us are affected in terms of higher costs and in a reduced ability to improve a health care delivery system because of decreased funding. On this side of the House we are not the only ones concerned about this as Liberal speakers have attempted to point out. They have suggested that perhaps we are panicking over a situation which they feel is well under control. However, all we have to do is look outside of the House to an organization known as Canadians for Health Research. That organization, which now consists of 200,000 people, was born approximately a year ago as a result of the emergency situation which exists in the area of health care and research funding.
My hon. friend from the Liberal side who has been wincing at my comments will soon be able to rise and explain. I am sorry, I do not know his constituency because he speaks so rarely in this place. Perhaps he can identify himself, Mr. Speaker. I will let him do so if he wishes. 1 understand he is a former scientist and will perhaps make his comments known.
We know that some 200,000 Canadians, lay people, people from various health professions and from all walks of life have demonstrated their concern at this government's lack of vision and understanding, by forming an organization known as Canadians for Health Research. Through such an organization they might increase the awareness of the public to the dirty deeds of this government and hopefully express the consternation of the research community to the public. By this method the government might be pressured in some way to change and reverse its negative role, a role which has been practised far too long.
No one says that research does not cost money. I certainly agree that it does. 1 contend that the benefits of research, as 1 have already mentioned, far outnumber the initial costs. In the past seven or eight years medical and scientific research in all fields in this country has been starved for lack of funding. The number of researchers and scientists has thinned out to a point where virtually no new people are coming into the research field because there simply is not the funding and there are no prospects of adequate employment in that area. This results in a deterioration of our research capacity together with a feeling of utter instability in the research community. We have a good peer review system in this country which reviews project applications on a regular basis in order to weed out bad projects. But the lack of funding is resulting in the cancellation
[Mr. Yewchuk.l
not only of bad projects but of excellent and productive projects which have already been under way, setting aside any exception for consideration of new projects or giving consideration to future projects submitted to the committee for approval.
Because of these Liberal policies basic research in Canada is becoming a dying field. Yet without it we all know that Canada can never hope to contribute internationally or even put to use its findings here at home to compete internationally.
Let me point out how important increased funding in basic and clinical research is by citing some examples of significant developments in the area of cancer research-colon cancer recognition by a blood test developed by Dr. Phillip Gold of Montreal; recognition of lung cancer antigens, a protein in the blood, which is of assistance to the diagnosis and perhaps treatment of lung cancer, developed by another researcher, Dr. Julia Levy of Vancouver; recognition of leukemia antigens by Dr. Michael Baker of Toronto. Similar work in the cancer antigen field is being done here in Ottawa by researchers at the Ottawa General Hospital, and perhaps other places. All these are very important contributions pioneered here in this country.
This year because of a substantial cut in research funding many of these projects will not be funded at all, or funded to such a low level that it is impossible to carry them on in a meaningful way. The result will be that this research will be done elsewhere. Because the work has been good and internationally recognized someone else will pick it up and do it. Canada will therefore remain at the bottom of the list of contributing western industrialized nations to this important field of research. Important, I might add because cancer has become one of Canada's top killers bar none. It is a serious disease and a serious problem and the government is freezing research in that area.
The former minister of science and technology has now gone to greener pastures with the National Capital Commission. He espoused the theory that each research program should be examined in the planning stage and, if it were cheaper to buy the results abroad than to carry out the work here, we should buy it. While that is perhaps a valid view for certain limited technical questions, I wish to list its fundamental flaws.
First, the less we do here the less we will be able to do here. Research cannot be turned on and off like a water tap in a sink. It will never be economical to carry out work here unless related work is being carried out here on a continuing basis.
Second, and perhaps this is the most important consideration against this idea or notion that you can buy research, is that no nation sells knowledge except as a loss leader. They sell products and services derived from those products and they are quite properly sold at a profit. The further loss of our economic independence would be reflected by an even worse balance of payments problem if the long range effects of "make or buy" are ignored. The decline of the research capability here means that foreign advances will be applied here incompletely
March 7, 1978

with lags of three to ten years. What I am attempting to say is that the economic and social costs of thinking we can buy research would be enormous.
Perhaps I can use the example of a new military weapon. A country might take the research position of Canada rather than a country like the United States which does a lot of research. Country A and country B may become locked in conflict. Country B may appear on the battle field with a new weapon that has not been seen before by country A. Obviously country B has been doing research and development. Country A might be able to go to country B and say they would like to buy their new weapon or they may try to get one, take it apart and attempt to build one of its own along similar lines, or improve on it. The battle would be lost before country A could develop such a weapon because of a time lag in such development which could be as much as three to ten years. If you are locked in battle and you need ten years to build a weapon to counter the weapon of your opponents, it is obvious who the winner will be.
That is the position in which the government has placed this country. In the area of scientific research and in all other areas of research we are taking a strange and backward approach. The results can mean nothing but harm to the public interest of this nation in the long run.
Let us take a quick look at the government's record in medical and scientific research funding. In 1975 Canada contributed only .9 per cent of the gross national product to research and development. During the same time the United States spent 2.3 per cent of its GNP. By early 1976, the actual federal expenditure on research and development had fallen to less than 0.5 per cent of the GNP. Of this 0.5 per cent spent by the government, only 0.1 per cent found its way to university research and only 0.1 per cent to industrial research, the two most productive areas for such expenditures. More current, a couple of weeks ago the Medical Research Council received their annual increase. Their principal budget for 1977-78 was $56.7 million.
The Minister of State for Science and Technology announced an increase of 7.8 per cent for the council bringing its budget for 1978-79 to $61.1 million. Even that announcement was dishonest, sneaky, underhanded, and misleading. Here's the catch. Last year the council received an added $1.1 million, a cost increase or borrowing against the future, which was substracted from the 1978-79 budget bringing the total down to $60 million, which represents an increase of 5.8 per cent not 7.8 per cent.
Even that is not an accurate reflection of what actually happened. An accurate reflection would be that that $1.1 million should be added to last year's budget because that is when it was spent, and reduced from this year's budget because it was not contained in it. The actual increase you come up with is 3.8 per cent. That is the actual increase in the medical research budget for this year, yet the minister had the gall to announce in his press release that this increase was 7.8 per cent. 1 cannot think of anything more despicable, and 1 can
Research and Development
think of a lot of despicable things to say about this administration.
Every year the budget of the Medical Research Council has been decreasing by about 10 per cent. 1 say that not only to reflect the actual gross increases but taking into consideration the cost of inflation. This increase of 3.8 per cent, matched with the erosion of funds by inflation, which in the medical research field is in the range of 15 to 16 per cent this year, leaves a clearly substantial cut in the budget.
If the Minister of State for Science and Technology were honest with the people of Canada, he would not be issuing a news release stating that there is an increase in the budget of the Medical Research Council. He would have stated that there was a cut in the MRC budget of approximately 10 per cent this year. That would have been a more accurate reflection of the facts.

My main message to the people of this country and the scientific community, particularly those involved in health research since that is the area of my responsibility for this party, is that if they want a change of policy, which I am sure they do, the only way to make that happen is with a change in government. This is the party that gave you extra time.

I shall be very brief in outlining the policy to which this party is committed and which will become government policy after the next election. Not only shall we be aiming to keep the level of funding up to previous years, taking inflation into account, but over the next five years it will be our intentions to catch up to the level of funding provided by other nations with which we shall be competing. speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although I may quarrel with what I consider to be the confining nature of the detail in the motion I do find much merit in the body of the motion. Indeed, it is my opinion, one shared by others, that it is crucial to the strength of Canada's economy

and the provision of employment opportunity that a vigorous program of technical research and development be promoted by the government.
I am one who believes we should be spending more and more on the development of new technology. If the bubble city of science fiction is ever to come into being, surely it will happen in our land where the environment of the north cries out for solutions. Surely we Canadians could be the first in the world to develop a new technology to enable all forms of life to grow, to live better and to exist together on this planet. The Russians and the Americans have set their sights on outer space, but hopefully they will look back from the moon and see Canadians bringing forward new technology not only to make our very existence on earth possible but to ensure that the earth itself has a more vibrant and glorious future.
In helping others we will help ourselves, for new technology brings about new job opportunities and never-ending spin-off of job situations which will ultimately do much to alleviate the problem of unemployment. New technology itself may be exported. In coping with our environment and the ills which befall human beings, plant and animal life, as well as with the sociological difficulties of living together, our research should lead the world.
At the outset I suggested that the five points in the motion are restrictive. As the Hon. Bud Drury once said:
A single science policy is not, however, a meaningful concept. What in fact exist are numerous policies for the use of science and technology, developed in relation to the objectives of federal departments and agencies and also in relation to objectives of the private sector.
1 find it hard to believe and intolerable that the motion makes no specific reference to university research. I note with interest that the present science minister, the hon. member for London West (Mr. Buchanan), gave high priority to university research in his remarks. I well remember, and with interest, that many of the speeches of the hon. gentleman's parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Maine), gave great support to the development of research in universities. Industries have their own facilities for research and development. Government, equally, has a need to provide such facilities. However, properly funded university research across the breadth of this country is able to serve industry, governments and all Canadians.
I realize that in this time of restraint great emphasis is placed on target-oriented research. There is also great emphasis on obtaining immediate results for each dollar spent. It would be a great error on our part, however, if we were to succumb entirely to these pressures. If we are to be the country of the future, then our future lies in true research. Our universities have been the ones which have clung to their academic purposes in the face of all pressures-with government support and without government support and with private support and without private support. Researchers have carried out their personal quest for knowledge in spite of all obstacles. I urge the minister to increase support so that great Canadian minds might remain in Canada and make a great
March 7, 1978

Canadian contribution for the benefit of all of us on planet earth.
Let me quote from a letter written to me on March 3, 1976 by Donald Sprung, Dean of the Faculty of Science at McMas-ter University. He wrote:
As a practising scientist, and dean of one of the most research-active science faculties in Canada, I fully share the concerns expressed by Professors Yates and Polanyi. Within our faculty the vast majority of professors are actively engaged in research. Many of them have national and international reputations for the value of their work. The high quality of my colleagues is reflected in the fact that at McMaster our research support from government and other granting agencies has not fallen as far behind as it has at other universities. Nonetheless, it has fallen in value, and by a considerable percentage over the past six years. These are just the years during which they are doing their best creative work, the years at which one would expect the level of support to be increasing. In fact, it is only in very rare cases that an individual has been able to secure an increase in funds.
Time and time again researchers across the country, professors and others, write to us to give advice and suggestions. Over the weekend I had the pleasure of being present for the Canada Jaycees Vanier Award to five outstanding Canadians. Among those honoured was Dr. John F. S. Crocker of Dalhou-sie University. He is noted for his research into Reye's syndrome. Dr. Crocker mentioned that we had gone through a period when it was considered fashionable to say: "Do not waste money; other countries are far ahead of us and we can either borrow or buy their research". In his own case a large amount of the funding for his research had to come from outside this country. We agreed that there is a marked change in that attitude, and there is every reason to believe that there is renewed interest in and sincere backing for Canadian research at all levels.
We must remember that federal funding of university research is necessary because of the importance of highly skilled scientists who are required to tackle problems facing Canada concerning the use of limited resources, population pressures, pollution and protection of the environment, health care, agricultural productivity and developing new sources of food and materials.
1 have had extensive dealings with the biology department at McMaster University. I would like to quote from some of the correspondence I have received from that department. This correspondence illustrates the understanding of that department of how this minister, his department, this government and others have responded in a real way to the requests of researchers across the country. Mr. Davidson, chairman of the biology department of McMaster University, wrote the following:
Our concern at the level of support for research is not only that our individual efforts as scientists are affected. As teachers, we also know that the approach active scientists bring to teaching is more critical and more alive because they have first-hand experience of contemporary problems in our knowledge. The active scientist is generally a more interesting teacher and is certainly a better informed teacher than a scientist who depends solely upon books for information. Thus our concern over research funding is not purely selfish; we see research as an integrated part of our teaching responsibilities.
Research and Development Professor Bayley from the same department wrote:
The human population is putting increasing demands on limited natural resources. To tackle the problems this creates, Canada like the rest of the world will require all the skilled scientific talent it can get. But maintaining and training skilled scientific talent means practising science "at the state of the art." With the sophistication of much of today's science, this cannot be done cheaply. If, to save relatively small amounts of money (by national standards), Canadian science is forced to lag behind, it will take years to recoup the lost ground. In the meantime, when up-to-date experts are required in Canada, the only reasonable step would be to import them from abroad. For a country of Canada's wealth and aspirations to continue to rely on imported scientific talent would be as unprincipled in my view as expecting other countries to provide us with trained medical staff-or hockey players.
Professor Douglas M. Davies of that same department wrote:
University research differs from government research ... in several important ways.
1)	Applications for university research grants are carefully appraised by specialists in each discipline ensuring that only the best is supported.
2)	Research at universities usually involves also the training of specialized graduate students who will be Canada's scientists of the future.
3)	A university teacher engaging in original research is able to bring to his teaching of undergraduate and graduate courses a first-hand excitement and freshness in presenting the latest in view scientific knowledge.
The head of that department, Mr. Davidson, seems to recognize not only our research problems but also our political problems. He wrote the following:
A problem for any government is to justify to the electors the allocations it makes of public funds. Thus, it would be easier for Mr. Trudeau's government to direct funds into, say, cancer and heart research, than into basic research on, say, wood production in eastern Canada, or fish breeding in northern Canada. But, as we tried to show you, the solution of problems unique to Canada will never be achieved in the U.S.A. or Europe. We have unique problems and to attack them we must, to some extent, be chauvinistic and parochial. We need a group of highly skilled highly trained scientists who recognize Canada's problems and are given the chance to work on them. To us, the solution is an adequate level of funding to support research.
All this and more has been said by researchers across the country, written to members of parliament and presented to the government and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
1 would like to note the fact that Max Chernesky, a virologist at St. Joseph's Hospital in Hamilton, along with Donald Savage, head of the Canadian Association of University Teachers, presented a report which is quite lengthy. However, there were three recommendations in their report, and 1 would like to tell the House how the minister, his predecessor and others have tried to respond to those recommendations.
One of the recommendations is as follows:
We recommend that governments at all levels consult with the organizations which represent professors and researchers prior to proposing new policies in higher education and, in particular, in regard to any negotiations between the federal and provincial governments over the financing of higher education.
The almost immediate response to that recommendation was the formation of the Canadian Committee on Financing of University Research. It is not a federal-provincial committee; it is a Canadian committee. This committee almost immediately stepped in to bring those forces together as a direct response to the brief presented by the Canadian Association of University Teachers. The committee was announced on November 2, 1976. It was announced that the committee

March 7, 1978
Research and Development
would be composed of 20 members; that the secretary of the Ministry of State for Science and Technology would be the chairman; that nine other federal officials, including the heads of the three granting research councils, would complete the federal representation; and that the provincial members would include deputy ministers responsible for universities, university presidents or principals or vice-presidents or vice-principals and representatives of university councils or commissions.
It was also announced that there would be a regional balance in the provincial contingent. The establishment of that committee marked the achievement of a new level of understanding and co-operation between the federal government and provincial governments in the matter of university research.
I now move to the second recommendation in that report which was produced in about February of 1976. The second recommendation was the following:
We recommend that government restore some of the lost purchasing power to the granting councils (the Medical Research Council, the National Research Council and the Canada Council).
There was an almost immediate response to that. Let us consider the estimates which have just recently been placed before us. The estimates provide for inflationary increases in the costs of research supported by the councils. The estimates tabled also carry forward into 1978-79 the additional increase of $8 million provided in the previous fiscal year and now adjusted for cost increases for programs relating especially to regional balance of scientific capability, national problem areas and the support of interdisciplinary research.
It is interesting to note that the budgets in 1978-79 will be: for the National Research Council, $105 million, an increase of $7.1 million; for the Medical Research Council, $60 million, an increase of $3.3 million; and for the social sciences and humanities program of the Canada Council, $31.1 million, an increase of $2.3 million. That is a direct response to a representation made by the Canadian Association of University Teachers.
The third recommendation is as follows:
While we would favour a change in the delivery system for the funding of universities and colleges, we recognize that the moment may not be propitious for such significant change.
This recommendation itself admits that it would be difficult at this time to engineer changes in delivery systems, but a direct response to this recommendation was the presentation of what was Bill C-26. That legislation has not as yet been proclaimed, but in time it will and it indeed makes a dramatic change concerning delivery systems. It does a great deal to bring forward some ideas which are a conglomeration of thoughts of people in many areas.
Granted, we have merely a reorganizational task at this point, but last session's Bill C-26, which was passed by parliament in June, 1977, has as its main thrust the creation of two new granting councils: the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council, formed by separating the support for university research in the natural sciences and engineering from the National Research Council; and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, formed by separating support
[Mr. MacFarlane.l
for university research in the social sciences and humanities from the Canada Council. The Medical Research Council was not reorganized by the bill, although its mandate was modified.
The three granting councils, NSERC, SSHRC and MRC, will be responsible for the majority of direct funding of university research by the federal government. Each of the councils will report to parliament through its own minister. The members of the councils and their presidents are appointed by the governor in council. The councils themselves are subject to certain administrative and financial constraints. Otherwise, the councils are free of government intervention and enjoy independence and autonomy. Neither the governor in council nor the designated minister can direct or instruct the councils. However, the minister may refer matters to the councils for advice.
Of course, the councils depend on the government for funds. In deciding on the amount of funding, the government will be influenced by the separation and revision of the councils. Therefore, it is only fair that the councils be made aware of the government's objectives and wishes. The manner in which they are conveyed to the councils is important and is being considered carefully.
In these few remarks I have been able to indicate my own desire to serve the research communities, my own confidence in Canadian researchers, and my own belief that we should be much more interested in all universities across the country which can, in a very real way, serve all of us by pure research in itself. All research must not be target-oriented. All research must not only be done on the basis of a dollar out is a dollar back, or a dollar out is ten cents back. Much research must be done on the basis that we have confidence in the minds in our universities and the minds the universities will have some participation in forming. No respectable researcher believes he is dealing with anything but plastic character when he deals with his students. He recognizes fully that he may be a sounding board, he may be somewhat of an example, he may open a few doors, but really he is dealing with the development of minds which will lead us on to much greater things in the future.
As 1 said at the opening of my short remarks, who else but Canada would be involved in the great plastic dome cities of the Buck Rogers world or the space world? Who else but Canada should really know how to deal with the environment? Who else but Canada will really have concern for those small pieces of life which exist on some of the islands in the north? Who else but Canada, sitting at the crossroads of the world between the United States, Russia and China, will have the responsibility for exporting not only technology but human technology? That is the technology which comes from the social sciences. As was mentioned earlier by an hon. member of the opposition, the basic idea is how we on planet earth can live together, healthy in a physical way, healthy in a mental way, and healthy in a way to exist on a planet so that we
March 7, 1978

ourselves do not bring about the demise of the planet. That is a great challenge for Canada.
I appreciate the fact that the motion has been introduced. I believe we are taking steps in the right direction. Perhaps some think we should move more quickly. I doubt if anyone thinks we should move more slowly. The hon. Minister of Public Works and Minister of State for Science and Technology has indicated direction. First, he responded immediately to recommendations placed before him; second, he established delivery systems which will ensure the involvement of all facets of the Canadian people; and third, he has shown a great recognition for the role our universities and research minds must play in any future which Canada wishes to lay any claim to at all.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane) presented what amounts to a total condemnation of the government's performance in science and technology. I compliment him on his speech. As he indicated by reading the record of his former colleagues at McMaster University, their community is less than happy with the government. 1 found the hon. member's comments rather interesting.

Order. At six o'clock the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) had the floor.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to participate in this debate. Since 1 have been here this is the fourth opportunity to discuss this subject on the floor of the House of Commons. Three of those opportunities were created by this party using one of our allotted days to indicate our concern and interest in this subject.
The recent history of the science policy in Canada can only be described as pathetic. By way of historic perspective it might be recalled that the first movement in this area occurred in 1919 when the Conservative government of Sir Robert Borden created the National Research Council. From that time until 1941 there was little concern or interest in a science policy. As a result of the interest created by the war, a Privy Council committee on science matters was created but in the period between 1950 and 1958 when the St. Laurent government was in office it did not meet even once.
Research and Development
In 1961, the Diefenbaker government introduced as a tax measure or 150 per cent write-off of incremental increases in research and development which had a very beneficial effect, but that measure was withdrawn by the Pearson government which, as a sop, created a science secretariat within the Privy Council.
In November of 1967, the other place created a special committee on science policy to look into such questions as recent trends in R and D in Canada; research and development carried out by the federal government; federal assistance to research and development; and the principles and structure of a science policy for Canada. This committee did an excellent job. I am not in the habit of praising the other place, but in this case 1 admit they did an excellent job.
I will not try to summarize the findings of that committee because they are rather extensive. Suffice it to say that they came out with three volumes, with a subsequent addendum, but their initial analysis was characterized by four rather profound and disturbing comparisons of Canada's performance. They concluded-this was in their first report in 1970- that Canada at that time invested a smaller percentage of its GNP in R and D than did most industrialized nations. They also concluded that of the tax money spent by the Canadian government, Canada spent a greater proportion on government labs than any other country of the western industrialized nation; that there was less spending on R and D in the private sector than in most industrialized nations; and that Canada spent a greater percentage of its R and D funds on basic research than did most industrialized nations.
That was the deplorable situation which existed in 1970. How has it changed in the last seven or eight years? Let us look at some figures. In 1967, Canada spent about 1.4 per cent of its GNP on R and D. The Lamontagne Committee recommended a goal for Canada of some 2.5 per cent as being appropriate. At the time the U.S. was spending 3.6 per cent, so they gave, as an appropriate target for Canada, something less than what the United States was spending. By 1971 the proportion of the GNP devoted to R and D in Canada had dropped to 1.2 per cent. By 1974 the figure had dropped to .85 per cent, and by 1976 this figure had dropped down to .8 per cent. In other words, a situation which was bad in 1967 became much worse seven or eight years later.
That performance can only be described as absolutely tragic for Canada, and there are a number of very good reasons why that is so. One of the foundations of a nation's future is its ability in the area of science and technology. Historians who like to pigeonhole epochs and areas describe this as the technological age. Obviously that is an accurate description.
How we use science and technology will clearly define both our standard of living and our quality of life. If governments feel they have a responsibility to the people and are concerned about our standard of living and quality of life-and I believe they are-surely they would give science policy a very high priority. Science and technology is vital to the performance of

March 7, 1978
Research and Development
any nation in areas such as trade. No economic unit can indefinitely buy more than it sells whether it be a family, a corporation, or a nation.
As a nation we have three commodities to sell to the rest of the world in order to generate the funds to buy the things we need but do not produce. Those three commodities are renewable resources, such as agricultural products; non-renewable resources, such as energy, minerals and the like; and our human value products or services. The latter can come in the form of brains or brawn. I do not think it desirable, nor do 1 think it possible, to expect Canada to compete with third world nations in terms of brawn. We cannot expect Canadians to endure the decrease in their standard of living that would be necessary if we were to compete with third world, low income nations for commodities and services in which sweat or back-power is the main component. This means that if we are to compete in the world marketplace in human value added materials, we have to do it in terms of brains, skill, talent or technology. In this regard Canada's performance is absolutely abysmal.
Last year our trade deficit in high technology manufactured goods was between $10 and $11 billion. That is an astronomical figure, but it is even more disturbing when you look at the trends. A decade or two prior to 1970 we ran approximately a $1 billion deficit-in constant dollars-in manufactured or high technology goods and paid for it easily with the export of agricultural products and non-renewable resources.
Since 1970 there has basically been a straight line deterioration in trade imbalance in manufactured, high technology goods from $1 billion to $10 billion. The trend is devastating and there has not been a single policy initiative from this government to try and arrest the trend or turn it around. If this is not done we are going to think that 10 per cent unemployment is nirvana compared to what we will experience in the future.
It is absurd in the extreme to have our officials in Switzerland talking about reducing tariffs and thus curing all our problems. The government has no apparent understanding of what is happening in Canada in terms of our deteriorating trade position. Cutting tariffs will only make a bad situation worse. We need a careful strategy, of which research and development is a fundamental element, to ensure that we can compete in the world. As long as we play "monkey hears nothing, monkey sees nothing, monkey speaks nothing," which is the posture the government has adopted, we will continue to have this kind of deterioration. Cutting tariffs will only speed the day when 15 per cent unemployment is the mean in this country.
In order to provide jobs for Canadians we must look to manufacturing, and that means high technology. We cannot compete with third world nations in manufacturing where there is a small skilled component. Primary industries simply do not create the jobs necessary to reduce unemployment. It is estimated that about 6V2 cents of every dollar from primary products goes into wages, whereas in manufacturing it is something like 35 cents of every dollar. For each dollar earned
[Mr. Andre.l
from manufacturing products there are six times as many jobs created as from the sale of primary products.
If the government is sincere about addressing the problem of unemployment, not just unemployment today but the unemployment we will have in the next three to four years, they should tackle the question of science policy and research and development and recognize that our performance in these areas is worse than any other industrialized country in the west.
That cannot be said often enough, Mr. Speaker. Our performance is the worst of all western industrialized nations. That cannot be blamed on international factors, on the weather, on the EEC, or on any of the unknown forces which seem to be causing all our other problems with dollars and so on. The fact is it is Canada's fault-the fault of this government.
What has this government done? When the Science Committee reported in 1970 the government quickly established a Ministry of State for Science and Technology to look after our problems. It was designed to generate policy, I assume. It generated one policy statement and that was the "make or buy" policy. It was a good policy designed to reduce the amount of government funded research conducted inside government labs. At that time, 1971, 62 per cent of all money spent by government directly was spent on research done inside government labs. As a result of that policy the figure has gone up to 65 per cent. So the one policy this ministry has produced in six years has had exactly the opposite effect to that which was intended.
I have said before, and I say again, that if that department were abolished we could save $6 million immediately. There are people in this country who think the government is concerned about science and technology just because there is a department with people making up to $60,000 per year sitting around thinking about science policy. People expect they will come up with great ideas because this government knows what is best for all of us and all these high priced people who are going to find out the answers. Mr. Speaker, they have produced nothing. I say we should get rid of them immediately. We would save that money and the attention of the public would not be deflected by that flim-flam.
I should like to elaborate a little on the problem that the government was trying to arrest with this policy, the amount of research being done in government laboratories, rather than in the private sector. I should like to point out for the benefit of the House the importance of research performed in the private sector. It is important not just from the point of view of the more efficient and effective action you get from the private sector as opposed to the government. It is also important because of the time lag between new discovery, innovation and implementation in a commercial way, which is greatly reduced.
As an example, Mr. Speaker, you have to look no further than the area around MIT and Harvard in Massachusetts, or the area surrounding Stanford and Berkeley in California, to
March 7, 1978

see the tremendous number of high technology industries, which have spun out of the fundamental research that has occurred at those institutions, research by and large funded by governments but performed in the private sector. If an idea is generated in the private sector, the time lag between idea and commercial application is greatly reduced. When those ideas are generated in government labs there is an unwarranted delay between discovery and implementation.
In this party our opinion is by and large, except for some areas where it may be necessary, that government should not do research and development. Government should sponsor research and development. They should help pay for research and development but they should contract it out to the private sector and not do it in-house.
We also believe that there is a role for government funding for fairly large projects. In addition, that activity can be used in a beneficial way. As an example, the largest research project of this century has to be the NASA program to put a man on the moon in the United States. As a result of powerful southern Senators primarily, but for other reasons as well, a good deal of the research money provided by the National Aeronautical and Space Administration went to companies and institutions which were located in the southern United States rather than the more developed northern United States.
In the southern United States, in the so-called sun belt, one of the effects of that benefit was to create tremendous growth of high technology industries, the net result being that regional discrepancies and regional economic differences between the north and the south were greatly reduced. What would happen if we took the $500 million a year that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is spending-to no avail because regional problems are getting worse in this country and not better-and we used that vast amount of money to create worth-while large scale projects which would be of value to Canada? The benefits would be considerable.
In the Canadian private sector in 1971 it was estimated that industry spent .41 per cent of the gross national product on research and development. By 1977 the figure had dropped to about .3 per cent. In other words, a very serious situation in 1970 had become much worse by 1978. The last budget of March 31, 1977 had a small tax credit for R and D activities of 5 per cent, rising to 10 per cent in the high unemployment areas. The United States, which is already doing four times as much R and D as Canada, has a tax credit of 10 per cent across the board. If the government was really interested they would be looking at tax credits in the area of 25 per cent, going up to possibly 50 per cent in areas of high unemployment.
Why is this so? Very quickly, I believe the answer was given by Dr. Robert Uffen, former head of the science secretariat that existed before the creation of the Ministry of State for Science and Technology. He said, and I am quoting from an article in Maclean's magazine:
The Trudeau government views science and technology as instruments for political manoeuvring both domestically and in international affairs.
Research and Development
That is dead accurate, Mr. Speaker. That is all this government recognizes science and technology for-as instruments for political manoeuvring. It is nice to go to Moscow and sign a scientific exchange to send a couple of scientists back and forth. It is nice, when one feels a little pressure about energy, to set up a research institute and say: "Hey, we are doing something'', and wave a flag. It is strictly a political instrument for the government's manoeuvring both domestically and in international affairs. There is no recognition whatsoever by the senior gurus in the government opposite of the importance of science to the long-term future of the government.
It is sad to say, but investments in science and technology have a long-term payout. Investment today may not yield a return for 5, 10, 20 years. As this government thinks only of next month's Gallup poll or next year's election it is not going to make that kind of investment in Canada's long term future. It is very sad for the nation, but that is the case. That is only one of a whole score of reasons why it is essential we get rid of them, and soon.
